# Why a positive screen is not a diagnosis

## Beat 1 — Two ways to test positive

Content needed: A hypothetical cohort of 1,000 contains 10 people with the condition and 990 without it. Blue means condition present; grey means condition absent. A positive result is a white outline, not a change in condition color. Nine of the ten with the condition test positive, a sensitivity of 90%. The false-positive rate is 10% among those without the condition. Before the pause, show the group sizes and rates but hide the count of false positives, the combined positive total, and the posterior probability. Reveal 99 false positives only after the pause. This is a toy probability model, not medical guidance.

Narration: Imagine a screening test in a hypothetical population of one thousand people. Ten have a condition, and nine hundred ninety do not. This is a toy probability example, not medical guidance.

Narration: The test catches nine of the ten people with the condition. That ninety percent is called its sensitivity. But it also gives a positive result to ten percent of people without the condition. Those results are false positives. A positive result can therefore come from either group.

Invitation (spoken): Which group will contribute more positive results? Take a few seconds to compare ten percent of nine hundred ninety with nine.

Pause: 4s

Reveal (spoken): Ten percent of nine hundred ninety is ninety-nine. The much larger group produces ninety-nine false positives, compared with nine true positives.

## Beat 2 — Choose the right group to count

Content needed: Preserve the identities and condition colors of the nine true positives and 99 false positives while regrouping them into one positive-results set. Remove negative results from the active view. Show 108 positive results in total, with nine blue marks and 99 grey marks at equal weight per person. Reveal 9 / (9 + 99) = 9 / 108 ≈ 8.3% in the order spoken. Contrast the reference sets for 9/10 and 9/108 without changing the nine true-positive identities.

Narration: Now suppose all we know about one person is that their result was positive. We should look only at the positive results. Bring the nine true positives together with the ninety-nine false positives. There are one hundred eight positive results altogether.

Narration: Of those one hundred eight, only nine belong to people with the condition. Nine divided by one hundred eight is about eight point three percent: roughly one in twelve.

Narration: Why isn't the answer ninety percent? Sensitivity starts with people who have the condition and asks how many test positive. Our question starts with people who test positive and asks how many have the condition. The nine people are the same, but the group we divide by changes from ten to one hundred eight.

## Beat 3 — Same test, different population

Content needed: Keep the first result, 9/108 ≈ 8.3%, as a compact reference. Introduce a different hypothetical population of 1,000 with 100 people with the condition and 900 without it: prevalence rises from 1% to 10%. Keep sensitivity at 90% and false-positive rate at 10%. Derive 90 true positives, 90 false positives, 180 total positives, and 90/180 = 50%. Do not depict specific people acquiring the condition. Preserve condition colors and positive-result marking. Present comparison as conditional on fixed test rates and the stated population model.

Narration: The starting proportion with the condition is called prevalence. Let's change it from one percent to ten percent in a different population of one thousand, while keeping both test rates fixed.

Narration: Now one hundred people have the condition. Ninety percent of them gives ninety true positives. Nine hundred people do not have it. Ten percent of them gives ninety false positives.

Narration: Among the one hundred eighty positive results, ninety have the condition: fifty percent, instead of eight point three percent. The test's sensitivity and false-positive rate haven't improved. The starting population changed.

Narration: Higher prevalence supplies more true positives and fewer false positives when those rates stay fixed. Lower prevalence does the reverse. To interpret a positive result in this model, count positives from both groups, then ask what fraction came from people with the condition.

plan.audience: Adults who know percentages but have not studied conditional probability.
prerequisites: Percentages describe parts of a stated group.
A fraction compares a part with its total.
plan.learningGoal: Calculate the fraction of positive tests that correspond to the condition and explain how prevalence changes that fraction when sensitivity and false-positive rate stay fixed.
plan.centralQuestion: Why can a positive result be unlikely to indicate the condition even when the test detects most people who have it?
plan.keyInsight: Positive results come from two differently sized source groups. The relevant denominator is all positive results, so a small false-positive fraction of a large condition-free group can outweigh true positives from a small affected group.
plan.runningExample: Toy cohort of 1,000: 10 with the condition, of whom 9 test positive; 990 without it, of whom 99 test positive. Sensitivity is 90%, false-positive rate 10%, prevalence 1%, and positive predictive probability 9/108 = 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. A deliberately constructed comparison cohort keeps the same test rates but has prevalence 10%: 100 with the condition yield 90 true positives, and 900 without it yield 90 false positives; 90/180 = 50%. Counts are idealized model counts, not measured clinical data.
misconceptions: Sensitivity is the probability of having the condition after a positive test.
A positive test has the same predictive probability in populations with different prevalence.
A fixed false-positive rate means the number of false positives stays fixed when prevalence changes.
The toy example provides medical advice or describes a real test.

entities.meaning: People with the condition, initially 10 in beat-1. Nine selected members become the true-positive subset in beat-1 and retain their identity through beat-2. In beat-3 this source-group representation explicitly describes a new comparison cohort of 100, not the same people changing condition status. Blue always means condition present.

People without the condition, initially 990 in beat-1. Ninety-nine selected members become the false-positive subset after the beat-1 pause and retain identity through beat-2. Beat-3 explicitly introduces a new comparison cohort with 900 in this category. Grey always means condition absent.

The positive subset of the condition group: nine in beats 1–2, preserving their condition color and individual identities during regrouping. In beat-3 the same category represents 90 positives in the explicitly different cohort. Each displayed person mark has equal weight.

The positive subset without the condition: 99 first revealed after the beat-1 pause, retained during beat-2 regrouping; beat-3 replaces these with the new cohort's 90. Grey is retained to distinguish actual condition status from test outcome.

Fixed selection rule: 90% of the condition group and 10% of the group without it test positive. White outlines indicate the positive result without changing condition colors. These two rates remain fixed throughout beats 1–3.
The derived fraction of positives with the condition, introduced in beat-2 as 9/108 ≈ 8.3% and retained as a compact reference in beat-3 while 90/180 = 50% is derived for the new cohort.

scenes.purpose: Show why the larger condition-free group can produce more positive results despite its smaller positive-test rate.
scenes.whyNow: Opens the explanation by defining the two source groups and test rates; establishes the counts needed for the positive-only calculation in beat-2.
keyPoints: Condition status and test outcome are different properties.
The rates apply to their own source groups: 90% of 10 and 10% of 990.
The larger source group contributes 99 false positives versus nine true positives.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because the inference concerns counts and set membership, with no spatial depth). On the black stage, introduce 1,000 equal person marks arranged as a countable schematic collection, partitioned into 10 blue marks with the condition and 990 grey marks without it; group counts make counting every mark unnecessary. Each mark represents one person, with no pictorial claim about real screening data. Use white outlines to select positive results while retaining underlying blue or grey fill. The true-positive and false-positive entities are subsets of these marks, not duplicate people. Establish the two source groups and rate labels first; outline the nine blue positives when spoken. During the bounded thinking interval, keep the grey group and its 10% label unchanged: no 99 label, selected grey subset, combined total, answer emphasis, or posterior formula. At Reveal, select exactly 99 grey marks and label both positive subset counts. Preserve these subset identities so beat-2 can regroup them without implying any change in condition or outcome. Exact layout is downstream; count labels must remain legible in the active safe region.
scenes.endsWith: Both source groups remain visible with positive selections: nine blue and 99 grey outlined marks. The rates and group totals are established; no combined positive total or predictive percentage is shown yet.

sourceRefs.supports: Population size, condition counts, positive counts, audience, brief thinking pause, and toy-example caveat; rates are arithmetic deductions from supplied counts.

scenes.purpose: Derive the probability of having the condition among positive results by choosing the correct denominator.
scenes.whyNow: Uses the nine and 99 positives just established to construct the relevant reference set; prepares the comparison of that fraction across prevalences in beat-3.
keyPoints: Condition on a positive result by retaining only positive marks.
The desired fraction is 9/108 ≈ 8.3%, approximately one in twelve.
Sensitivity divides the same nine by 10, whereas the requested probability divides by 108.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because selecting and regrouping sets directly exposes the denominator). Begin with the actual beat-1 end state. Move the same nine blue and 99 grey selected marks together, preserving one mark per person and their condition fills; remove the unselected negative marks from the active view. A white enclosing boundary defines the positive-results reference set only as narration identifies it. Introduce 108 after assembling both subsets, then build the yellow fraction 9/(9+99), simplify to 9/108, and display approximately 8.3% with the corresponding spoken calculation. For the sensitivity comparison, use compact labeled count relationships rather than duplicating the full cohort: the shared numerator nine is tied to the same blue subset, while reference-set labels distinguish all 10 with the condition from all 108 positives. Keep rates as a quiet reference. End the comparison by removing redundant sensitivity arithmetic and retaining the single positive set and derived fraction. No later prevalence values appear early.
scenes.endsWith: One positive-results set contains nine blue and 99 grey equal-weight marks, with total 108 and the derived 9/108 ≈ 8.3%. The two fixed test rates remain available for the next scene; original full source groups have exited.

sourceRefs.supports: Request to derive the positive-test probability of the condition; 108 total positives and 9/108 are deductions from the supplied nine and 99.

scenes.purpose: Explain how prevalence changes the composition of positive results even when both test rates remain fixed.
scenes.whyNow: Uses the established positive-only denominator and retains its first result for comparison; concludes by showing how to repeat the reasoning in another population.
keyPoints: Prevalence describes the starting fraction with the condition.
A new hypothetical population changes prevalence from 1% to 10% while fixing sensitivity at 90% and false-positive rate at 10%.
The new group sizes yield 90 true and 90 false positives, giving 50% among positives.
For these fixed test rates, increasing prevalence raises the true-positive contribution and lowers the false-positive contribution.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because a controlled numerical comparison isolates the effect of prevalence). Start with beat-2's positive set and fraction. Retain the original fraction as a compact labeled 1%-prevalence reference, and deliberately retire its person marks before introducing a different cohort; do not animate individuals acquiring the condition. Reintroduce the blue and grey source-group categories with 100 and 900 people, represented by proportional count bars on a shared population scale summing to 1,000. Explicit labels show this is the new cohort. Keep the 90% and 10% test-rule labels unchanged. Select 90 of the blue group and 90 of the grey group using the white positive marking; these can be regrouped as equal-length positive-count bars on one shared scale. Reveal total 180 and fraction 90/180 = 50% only as calculated in speech. Use the old 8.3% reference to compare probabilities without retaining a second thousand-person drawing. For the final directional inference, hold the source group sizes and their fixed-rate relationships visible: more people in the blue source yields more blue positives, and the complementary grey source shrinks. Do not suggest the test rates were estimated anew or that this model applies unchanged to a particular medical test.
scenes.endsWith: The new cohort's two positive contributions are equal at 90 each, with 90/180 = 50%; a compact reference records the original 1% prevalence and 8.3% result. Both fixed test rates remain visible, grounding the concluding dependence on prevalence.

sourceRefs.supports: Requested explanation of changing prevalence while holding sensitivity and false-positive rate fixed. The 10%-prevalence comparison is an explicitly constructed teaching example, and its counts are deductions, not additional supplied data.
